explanation: The exception hierarchy is a class hierarchy (2.5). Catching a base catches all derived - which is why order matters.

explanation: First match wins and Exception matches everything, so C# rejects the ordering outright - a polite guardrail.

stem: catch (HttpLikeException ex) when (ex.StatusCode == 404) - the advantage of the filter over catch-test-rethrow:
options: A declining filter never UNWINDS the stack - unhandled exceptions keep their original throw point for the debugger
explanation: Filters decide WHETHER to catch. Catch-then-rethrow destroys context; a filter that says no was never there.

stem: Inside a catch block, 'throw ex;' instead of 'throw;':
options: RESETS the stack trace to this line - the trail to the real failure is destroyed
explanation: The lesson counts surviving stack frames to prove it. The analyzer flags it (CA2200); the bare 'throw;' preserves everything.

stem: Catching IndexOutOfRange and throwing DataLoadException(message, inner) - why pass 'inner'?
options: InnerException preserves the ORIGINAL cause and trace while callers see a domain-level failure
explanation: Translate layers without losing evidence: the user-facing message up top, the full chain underneath for the debugger.

stem: InsufficientFundsException carrying Balance, Requested and Shortfall properties lets catchers:
options: ACT on the data - suggest the maximum withdrawal - instead of parsing a message string
explanation: Write a custom type when callers might HANDLE your failure specifically; carry the facts as properties, not prose.

stem: You need to signal 'caller passed a negative count'. Best choice:
options: The built-in ArgumentOutOfRangeException - it already says exactly this
explanation: Prefer built-ins when they say it: Argument..., InvalidOperation..., NotSupported... Custom types earn their keep only for domain-specific handling.

options: if (player is null) throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(player)); - one line for the standard guard
explanation: ThrowIfNull, ThrowIfNegative, ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace - the boundary guards (4.5) as one-liners, parameter name captured automatically.

stem: Failure is a NORMAL expected outcome (user typed a bad number). The right tool:
options: TryX / return false - exceptions are for exceptional paths, and they are slow
explanation: Contract broken -> throw. Wrong state -> InvalidOperation. Normal failure -> Try pattern. The 1.11 timing (hundreds of ms vs ~1) still applies.

stem: catch (Exception) { } - an empty catch-all - is harmful because:
options: The bug RESURFACES later, elsewhere, with all evidence destroyed
explanation: If you cannot handle it, do not catch it. Swallowed exceptions become mystery corruption three functions away.
